blocks.x: I'll make a note on here first that we're interviewing kid Jimmy Clayton at his home, and the date is June the 23rd, I believe, is it? 1961. What is the address? How do you say the street? It's 3316 Leandes. Leandes.
Well, I don't know, that's just... Just comes natural. Just comes natural.
Yeah, that's holding it so hard, that right now.
Much better, that way. Yeah.
That's right. Some people have it down like they're blowing at the ground. That's right.

I always have my head up. That's a picture... Let me see, who took that picture? Did you take that picture? I was down in the country, went down there, and laid the droves down there. I forget her name. She had a moipery. And she went down there, a picnic where we played. That's way down in Diamond, Louisiana.
No, I don't think so.
I thought she went with us. Because we left, they met us right there at St. Philip and Claiborne, and we went in her car.
When was this? When about was this? How long was this? Let me see, it was around 56, I believe.
If I'm not mistaken.
No, I don't think it was. It might have been, but I don't remember. I wonder if it was Mr.

What was this other man, Mr. Just a second. Nick Allen. I don't even hear what you're saying. This Blaine machine is going bum. Remember the one that used to get a hum on it, Ralph? We sent the other mic away yesterday. It's working now, I see. Yeah, it's working all right. Yeah, but still look where it is when there's nothing on it. Everybody keep quiet just one second. See? Yeah, we got a hum on it. Got a hum on it again. Guess we'll have to go to the shop. Anyway, it'll pick up what we say, but there's going to be a little hum along with it.
Looks like you're singing a number here.
I am singing.
Oh yeah. I'm singing Don't Take My Gat Out Fishing.
What's that, a blues?
Just like a blues. It's got a brakes in it, and it's great. It's one of my makeup.

One of your numbers. That's a good picture. Let's see, if we go through these other pictures here. This is some of the old, you call this picture is Hummingbird Stomper. Yeah. This is John Hande. When was this taken? It looks like a fairly late picture.
This was taken last year. Yeah. We've got a group.

It's Alec Beegard and George Gayneau. Hande and Lester San Diego. Okay. Yeah, it's a very picture. There's one thing I might do here. I don't think it'll help much. Let me turn the plug. There's always a chance. I believe that helped it. Sometime a certain one of the wires is grounded better than the other. Oh yeah. Seems to be going better. Yeah. Okay, so we won't have to worry about it now. Sorry for the interruption. We have plenty of time. Sure. Let's see, what are we talking about again? Some of the other pictures there? Anything else to go through any of those pictures right off you? I don't think so. No, I guess not.
You were working out at Gramercy there about four or five years ago. Yeah, around 57. Yeah.
What were you doing out there?
Carping there? Carping the helper.
Uh huh.
Do you do a lot of that kind of work?
Well that's the, yeah, you know what I mean. When the locals send me out there, they put me with the carping.
Oh I see, you were with the locals. Yeah, I went with the locals.
Well that's a good job.
There is something like that, to take care of the vacant spots.
That's right, sure. Because you know, you can't make it on music. I got to make it some kind of way. Yeah, that's right.
Do you find times to be pretty tough now for music?

Well I'm going to tell you this, it's really tough. I ain't played a job since I played that little two hour job on a parade that's, when was that? The Southern School? Yeah, the Southern School, yeah, that's right.
That's the last job you played, huh?

That's the last job I played. And my father was there while I went and played a few numbers for my daddy, we gave him a little party. That was nice. And we circled around. I sure wish I could have touched with you, you could have, yeah. Yeah, like a serenade, huh? Yeah, a serenade. So we left him there and went down with Paul, some of his relations down next to the Union Hall. What was that, Paul, Paul who? Paul, Paul.
Paul, yeah? Yeah. Well, they don't do those things like that very much anymore.

I never had done them. They sure don't. Well, we'd do it, you know what I mean, I'd do it with him. So we left him there, went on Padilla Street, but the people I was with, they had to go home, you see. So I brought them home, and when I come back I believe he was gone. I left him, Bigfoot Bill, you know Bigfoot Bill, a drummer. Oh, he's great. You always see him get on his knees and play that bass drum.
Crawling and do everything.
He's a great drummer. And, well, Paul plays with me right regularly now. Paul Barrett?
Yeah. Oh, wonderful.
He plays with me right regularly. Anything I get, I call him, you know, he'd come right on up there.

Yeah. I was gonna ask about some of the other old time days and the jobs you played, like, they tell me they used to have, every time they'd have a wedding party or a christening or a birthday or anything else, they'd have a band in the old days. That's right. And they don't do that now. They got a jukebox or nothing at all, radio.

That's right. They don't hide a band. I used to get so much work, though. I used to have to turn down some, either get a, you know, sub it out to some other band. I used to be going all the time. Things got rough here now.
Did you ever play out at Millenburg? Oh, yes.

I used to play out there every Sunday, Saturday. We was playing at the Law Cabin or either at Sam's Camp, and people used to be like that. Sometimes the tires would come in and we had to walk in water about a mile to get to the road. Really? Yeah, the tires would come in backwater, you know. Did they come over the boardwalk? That's right, come over the boardwalk. We had to walk in the water. Oh.
That's right. I didn't know. Did they flood the little camps, the buildings?
That's right. Flood, they'd flood them. We had to come out there.
That wasn't the regular tide each night or did you see?
No, it was just...
Like a hurricane guy or something.
Yeah, like that or something. Something up higher. Right. And I used to play out at Mama Lou. You ever been out there?
Oh, yeah. I used to go there a lot.
Well, me and Andrew Jefferson, we had the band there.
They didn't go there a lot because they cut it out there a few years ago. Yeah, after she died, yeah.
She died or so. She was a good woman. She had a gold spot right there. Yeah. They had some other people, in-laws try to take it but they couldn't come up to the seafood, you know, like she did.
In 56 or 57, the other people took it over and it didn't last through the summer.
That's right. And the happy land I used to play out there with Israel going. Oh, yeah.
That's not going anymore either, is it?
No, I think that people died out there.
That was going about two years ago and then they quit last year. They quit, yeah.
Well, I left Israel out there.
Well, I heard you way out there farther down the lake, that was 1951 I remember.
That was down at Mary's Camp, yeah. That's the last camp down out in the water.
Yeah, I haven't been down there since, and since then they built Lincoln Beach I guess. Or was Lincoln Beach already there? Do you remember?
Let me see, yeah Lincoln Beach was there.
Well where is Lincoln Beach then?

I don't even know in relation to Mary. It's like you're going, you go past Mama Lewis and keep straight on the next stop is to Lincoln Beach. And then when you go straight on now, Mary's Camp, when you make that right turn to come. And Mary's Camp is farther down in Lincoln Beach.
Yeah, that's right. I thought maybe that's the same as Lincoln Beach now where you played before.
No, no, that's Mary's Camp.
That was farther then.

That's farther then. Guess there's no music down there now at Mary's? No, they cut up so bad I'm going to tell you. Last time I played down there, them boys got to fighting and we started playing music, thought it would stop them. Man, somebody put the lights out. Somebody throw the table, and the table come over there by me, and I sat down behind the music box and it paid off like a slot machine, you know when you hit the jackpot, ding-a-ling-a-ling. Because you grabbed the money. No, I sat there and my brother-in-law here in Baton Rouge, he'd come out and hear me play, and he'd sit on my head. I said sit right there, that's all right. He'd sit on my head. He'd sit on my head. I ain't never seen a man pack up a pair of drums and crawl out with him. See Abbey? Well Abbey was there. Abbey was there. That's right, he was playing with you when I was. I laughed until I cried. Abbey was running in the toilet there with his drums and he couldn't go no further, you know. He was just a boy now. But it was rough. Oh, it was rough down there. But we had the police when we come that next week and heist them all like a wrecker.
I remember a lot of young kids, like high school kids all the time I was there. That's right.
They sure they'd fight and kill. The women's too. Pick up tables, Troy, that one night.
Yeah.
And so I told my brother-in-law, I said you sit on my head, you ain't hurtin' me, I didn't want to get hit. I could stand his weights, you know.
I was going to ask a little bit about some of the brass bands that you've played in. Any regular band or just jobbing around different bands?
Well I played with, he's dead now, what is his name, he lived downtown, I believe he had the Supreme Band if I'm not mistaken. He was a good trumpet player, tall and bright fella.
I can't call his name. It's been Maurice Burand.
No, I know Maurice Burand, I used to play with him too.

He was sort of tall and heavy too, he is now. Well he died. No, he's, I think you went to San Francisco, we saw him two years, about three years ago and he was dead. Moran? Big Fat Moran? No, no, that's Herb Moran. Boyd Moran, yeah he's dead. Maurice Duran.
Oh Maurice Duran.
The Ninth Ward on Lazardi Street.
Yeah, I think he's living there. Yeah, he's out in California.
Yeah. Did you ever have a brass band of your own, Jimmy?
No, I didn't have a brass band. If people would hire me I'd just call up the Eureka or John Cashmere and I'd play with it. That'd be my band right on.
That's right.
Yeah, I'd get jobs, I played right with them.
Do you remember any of the real old time bands like the Onward and Excelsior?
Yeah, Excelsior, yeah. I played with a lot of them old fellas in the Excelsior brass band, Excelsior's jazz band too. I played with all of them, every band in town.
He was mostly in the Excelsior band. Do you remember the leader or anybody, the main ones in the brass band? Wooden Joe was in the band.

He worked? He worked in the band too. If he'd have been living, he was a great trumpet player. Yeah, I knew him very well. I'd be strong. You know? He was about the most powerful man in town. That's right.
He sure was powerful.
You get him on the parade you can hear him.
I'm telling you.

And well I done played with every band in town. I just played with Dan Moody from Bugalusi. Oh yeah. He died. Big Dan, yeah. He had a wonderful band. We used to go on the road. all on the coast, Mississippi, Louisiana, all around. I remember one night we was playing in Hazelwood, Mississippi. Cold, cold one night. So after we played the dance we'd come to, we were still in the hall, so we made a big fire. So we couldn't get, didn't want to go awake, nobody had to get a room you know. So we decided we'd take the top wing out the bus, lay it on the floor, we lay down there you know, on the floor. Then we made a big fire, one of them big old rangers you know. You could put your foot around the ranger. I don't know, my head was kind of bad you know. I could stand there and go to sleep, it must have got good to me, I went to put my foot up you know like that, and stuck it on that hot fire. Oh I couldn't put my shoe on. I longed the whole parlor. Dad showed me the floor, they had to bring me to the hospital, I blessed my feet. You know stuck on it. That can be red hot or stones. That's right. And Bob had been drinking a little bit too you see. So I couldn't get, and I had to pair a flo-shine shoe, that's all I wear was flo-shine shoes, and they were tight. So I had to go slip and put on that foot.
Yeah, that'd be painful, that'd be hurt and soft.

And I don't know whether George ever told you this. No, no. We was in Crystal Spring, we was going, we hadn't been to the hall, coming back. I know we thought we'd take the shot because we were with some girls you know. And I jumped down the clip, we both fell down the clip. Me and me. He never told you about it? I went down the clip, the saxophone player went down the clip, and my trumpet, I bent my trumpet, he broke the neck off the banjo, and pointed out, bent his saxophone, and Jose, the bass player, you know Jose, he was the bass player. But he fixed it. He fixed that, put that banjo together, and he straightened my horn out and he went on, he played out music.
It was great. Yeah, lucky they got prepared that.

It must have been about a ten or fifteen foot jump. It was dark, you see. It looked like I was stunning myself, you know, coming right down on my feet, all of us, the whole bunch of, while we had been drinking, you know, too, you see. And we used to play all over Mississippi. One night we was in Columbia, Mississippi, and I was playing with Abby, two that night, one Christian's night. And he gives the man my ticket, and I goes on off, you know, with a girl, and they all left me. So when I was a freshman I went back to get my horn and my overcoat, I fell for my ticket, I had no ticket. So the lady said, there go your bus now. I said, that's the bus going to New Orleans? She said, yeah. I said, I saw a place where you're catching. She said, you got to go about eight miles. You know I run that eight miles, I got that bus. I run eight miles. You must have been in good shape. Oh yeah, I was young, I could go, you know. I was running, I'd run off the road, I'd run in the road, I kept, I was watching that taillight, you see. So was that bus. I followed. When that bus got there and it was loading up, I got there, I was steaming, but I got there. I looked at him and I was so mad at him. And we got on the bus and we come on into town and the bus kept swerving. I told the driver, I said, I went up there and told him, I said, you better stop your bus and check your tires because you're going to turn over. He felt it going, you know, dancing all over the highway. So I told him and he pulled on the side and stopped the bus around Salt Bay on 11. And they rang up and they sent another Greyhound to pick us up.
You were on Greyhound? Yeah, we was on Greyhound. In those days I guess they weren't so modern anyway. No they weren't so modern.

So all the other people, they wanted to get on ahead of us, so the bus driver told them and said no, so let these musicians get on first because if it don't be for him, none of us would have got home, see, we'd have turned over, you know, off the highway. So we got in the bus and sit down and put our instruments up and come on into town. But I can tell when them cars go to swing, you see, that's it, turn over right now. But I done been in a gang of them on the road. But just luck enough I didn't get quite too bad. I've been in six racks. Really? That's right. One night we was coming from Vachery, Louisiana, on that old river road, and I told the fellow, I said, listen, I said, you're driving on the wrong side of the highway. I said, keep to your right. All ain't nothing coming. Just then there come a truck. Shooting around the curb and I grabbed the wheel and we took the ditch. Turned over and the drum player he broke his ankle. Who was that? We called him Lagre Mas, I forget this little fellow, he was a little Creole fellow that lived downtown. And he broke his ankle. All of us could have got killed. Didn't get a scratch on him. But we lucky. Turned over the whole truck. I mean turned over, running the ditch. Well I had to do that because he'd had a head on. Oh yeah, he'd get killed. So I always stay awake when I'm driving. Or whoever's driving I always watch him, you know, because he's staying up. I'd have been in all kind of wrecks. After all, I was a kid. I'd have been in all kind of wrecks. After all those wrecks I don't blame you. I played music too. I've seen us, we come from Picayune, I used to play at the end of Picayune Jones' Jewry Store. And we was coming home, it was raining. I lived down here on Cleveland Street. And I told the fellow, I said, now look, I said, watch these corners. He said, okay. We got to the corner here, a fellow slid right into us, boom, and hit us and we run up in the barbershop. Didn't get no scratch on me again. I said, must be a...
You ran your car up into the barbershop? Yes, indeed.
Through the window? It hit us right up in the door.
Oh, okay.
I said, Lord, I'm a kid. There it is again. Lucky again.
Yes, indeed.
Well, out of all that we come out, God's good, we. Yeah? Ain't got broke up yet.

Yeah. Are there any other jobs you can remember? Well, I know you played hundreds and hundreds of places, I'm not going to try to make you remember all of it. Any longer engagements, any particular place?

Well, the longer engagements, let me see, I was at the Humming Boy and then out at Mamalu. But after I went to the army and come back I went out there and worked. And the time we was working out there, before the war, we was getting about two and a half a man out of tips. But the tips was great. Each man would make around about fifty, sixty, seventy an hour. Besides that little two and a half a night it paid. But after I come out the army I wouldn't play for that no more. I made her raise the price. So she raised the price and I played for until she gave the place up.
How many years were you there altogether?
Oh, I was there way before the war. During the Depression time.
Back in the middle of the morning?
Come out to WPA man. Oh yeah.
You really had that job. Oh yeah, we had.

We had that job every Saturday and holidays. Every Saturday and holidays. And she had a good place. All them jurors just come from out there and they tip us great. Five, ten dollars, fifteen, twenty. Captain DeLatchy used to come out there. He wanted to give us a hundred dollar bill, his wife snatched it out of my hand. He don't know what he's doing, give me this money back. And he was a bass player himself, Captain DeLatchy, you might know him. No, I don't know him. He was on the 40s floor. Yeah, I don't know. And he liked to get in there with us, you know, he'd take the bass, he'd say, yeah he said, he had a hundred dollars. Oh, what did he care, he was getting the money. A lot of grabs. Grabs, yeah, see. So he'd give me a hundred dollar bill, his wife snatched it in front of him. He don't know what he's doing, he's drunk. He said, I'll give you some money. Oh, I said, yes ma'am.
I was going to ask a little bit before we've only got a couple more minutes to start on here, but anything about your lessons you can remember that old man up is Jim Humphrey
and he said, yeah well, we took lessons from him and after he'd taken sick, well he didn't give them no more, we'd get around there and do it ourself, you see.
Remember anything like, did he have certain books or when he'd teach you alone, did he have a method book?

Yeah, he had a method first, but I don't know what, I had one of them I told language messages. Oh, good. Yeah, yeah, yeah. I had one of them with all the fingering marks on it. Yeah, I had one of them.
Did he ever teach you about the beat, the tall, the counting and patting your foot or
everything? Yeah, patting our foot, you know, and when you peel walls and you know. Slide it over and stuff. Yeah.
One, two, three.

Yeah, all that, he taught us all that. But when you started playing out did you forget all about that? Oh, we didn't need that. I just went on for myself then. I went on for myself. I learned to punch how to play Muscat and Ramble. Oh really? Yeah. He was playing with Miramak Makershul. And they come down and the lyrics come here. So he come over and see me and said, I told him, I said, come on, rush me up for some punch. He said, I want to play the Muscat and Ramble. I said, I'm going to show you how to play it. See, because we'd get Louis Armstrong's records and go over them a few times and everybody had their part where they had to play it. And we played it. And I learned how to play the Muscat and Ramble. And they sure wanted me to go away with them. Well I believe he jumped them in Houston and come back to New Orleans. Yeah, that's right. Yeah, he left them in Houston and come back to New Orleans. So they come back to get me. And I wouldn't go because I done been all out there. I ain't going on the road to starve. I had to eat blackberries, man. Sometimes you had money in your pocket and couldn't get nothing to eat.
Oh yeah, that's right.

That was tough. Stop on the road and eat watermelon. Anything you could see to eat. Corn, anything. Sugar cane, anything. That's true. Old bus break down and we walk. And I used to play with Earl Foster too. We used to play at Skinner's place out in Buccalus. Oh he had a Cadillac with crepe-de-sheen ties. Now he had to be there at work for nine o'clock and leave here at eight o'clock. Now he'd go across the bridge, you know how he lived? Like the tunnel over in the lake, the tie busted and all of them. Right on that whole bridge thing. Oh Jesus, it scared me from that. All right we get some slide there, we fix the tie, and we say, well Earl, you fix the tie so we're going to walk. You know, we get on the walk on the highway. We walk, we walk. So we walked on down there, about five or six acres, and some dogs, about a hundred dogs got behind us. I was leading the crowd. So Earl caught up with us down the road, and we got in the car and we all was holding, fingers crossed you know, and got up the road a little piece of the tie, let out again. Boom! I said, oh Lord, hold on. He said, don't worry, we're going to get there. I said, we're going to get out and walk some more. We got out and walk. He fixed the old car, got back in the car again. After he picked us up, I said, I guess we'll get there now and be riding back, sitting down there, whole crane and everything. So after a while you know, he got in the curve there and there come a horse cutting across the highway and he hit that horse. And there it was again, the horse went up there and come right back down on the windshield and rolled over the top and all of us was full of horsemen in there. Wow.
So I told him, I said. Were those open cars or something those days, or what were they like?
No, he had old hardtop Cadillac, one of them old miles.
That's a hardtop.
Yeah, he had to pump it to make the fuel come up to it, you know.
Yeah, I remember that.

Yeah, that's an old Cadillac you had. And them lights you couldn't see, they were old counter lights, like counter power lights. And I said I quit playing with her from that day, I said, if I go with him I'm going to take my own car, you see. And that's what I did, I'd take my car and make him pay me transportation to bring my car. I said, no, you take your men in the car, I'm going to go in my car. But them fellas they want to drink too, you know what I mean, see, and you can't drink and drive. No, I'm kidding.
Yeah, it's kind of tough on the road all right, you don't do that anymore Jim?
No, no, I don't do it anymore. I don't like the road no more.
No, I don't really.
I don't like it.
Did you ever go any big trips like to Chicago and play anything else in the world?

Well, I used to play around Chicago. I used to play around there when Lewis was there. I used to play at the Red Mill, Green Mill. I used to play at the Dancing Academy on Vincent Avenue. I used to boom with Lewis there. Oh yeah? Yeah, we used to be together at the Vendom, we used to play there all the time. And we used to play down 35th Street at Royal Garden. Royal Garden? Yeah. The Sunset, I believe.
Sunset. Sunset 35th.
Yeah, 35th.
Royal Garden on 31st.
Yeah, 30th. That's right. I played all out on Boyntons Avenue.
How long were you in Chicago?

I stayed off and on there. I was around there at 22. I left around, see but I was stationed in the Barberton, Ohio. I had a little tavern job in Akron I was playing every night, 85 East North Street. I played piano and laid my trumpet on the top of the piano. Well I started to ask if there's any other instruments you ever played except your ukulele or all that. Yeah, I played piano too. So I got me a girl who played piano in Wadsworth, she lived in Wadsworth, and her brother played drum well and we made up a little three piece combo, you know, as in Akron, Ohio, right behind the Goodrich Rubber Company.
That part of playing rugby?

Oh yeah, I've been all over the state of Ohio, Pennsylvania. I made good money just with my little combo. When I come back to New Orleans, well that's where I got famous then, you see, after I got here and everybody knew that I was back in town. I got jobs. We used to go all through Texas. We had a porter used to catch us on the train, see. They used to take the whole band nine minutes for 35 hours. And you'd ride the train. Used to get jobs all in Galveston, Houston, Orange, Texas. I never want to go back there no more. What happened there? We was in a truck, advertising, you know like you go around Ballyhorn, and they had some fellas following us. And so I said, these fellas following us, like the band might give us a job or something. So when we got on the outskirts, we didn't have no house like Suesbury, you know, from New Orleans. They pull up and asked the fellas, he said, stop the truck. So he stopped the truck and he said, get out. So he said, you got your gun? He said, no, I don't have my gun. He said, lie me a chance. And they shot him in the road and asked us which one of us could drive the truck. I told them I could drive the truck. Wait a minute, they shot who? Shot the driver. I don't know, it must have been a whiskey deal or some kind of deal. I was so scared, I never do want to go to Orange, Texas no more. They shot the driver? Yeah, killed him and told us to leave him in the road. I said leave him in the road.
I said, y'all go ahead and play your music.
And that night we played with them guys, I said, I said, I said, I said, I said, I said, I don't want to eat an orange no more. You guys come up there with horses, you know, on horses, in the hall.
In the hall?

I was riding them cowboys, you know how them cowboys, they rough. I said I don't want to eat orange no more. I don't eat orange no more. Don't hear nothing about orange touches. They had us playing Casey Jones and the Black Cat and everything. I played it. I was scared too, I'm telling you. I said when I get out there I'll lie, I ain't coming back.
You've got to believe it. That road's a tough thing, I wonder you don't go on that road.

No indeed I give the road up, I give it up. Yeah, I don't know, I'm going to try to get back on Boyle Street if I get a break. If I get a break I'm going to try to get out there. Rick and I tried to get me to play with him at the Mardi Gras. But see I was working out there, you see at Bramson, I couldn't stay at them hours a night, you know what I mean?
No, it was a long ways out there.
Yeah, that's right. And then I was making good money out there too. My money was a hundred and sixty something dollars a week. Besides my riders I used to carry.
Yeah, that was nice.
Yeah, it was a nice job. I worked with Mr. Zardo.
That same job you were on?
Yeah, that same job, because he looked for me and he found me. He was surprised to see him out there, I was glad to see him.
Yeah, I think it was she told me you were out there. Yeah.

I just looked for him to the house. He sure looked until he found me. He found me, we talked, talked, everything was lovely. Yeah. Yeah, that's my market out there. I bought it on that job up there. Oh yeah, that's right, yeah.
Yeah, that was a good job on.
And I worked another good job down here at the England Oil Company down there.
Oh yeah?
For an out of town company. Money was another two hundred a week.
Yeah.
There was really some great people.
Some of that beats playing music but still aren't there.
Oh yeah, it don't last long.
It don't last long. Once you play music you don't want to give it up.
No, I ain't going to give up my music because I can make it in music when I don't be working.
Yeah, those jobs, they could while they last but they don't last long. They don't last long.
They don't last long. They just enough to get you in debt and... Yeah.
That's right. You lose money in the animal military. That's right. That's right.
Well, you're just about out of tape. Is there anything else that you can think of about your life that you'd want to tell us? If not, why we can...

Well, I'm going to tell you, I come up the hard way and I got my music and I went and played this band, I'll tell you on the coast there, Auguste Associates. We used to play at the Reeds Hotel, you might know right at that light, there's one light.
Oh yeah? How far over?
That's in Bay St. Louis.
Bay St. Louis?

Yeah, right about across. It's a light. Well we played there. And I used to get the drummer, he used to go out of town with me, George used to go with me, and I used to send Albert Fernandez, you know him? Yeah. I used to send him over there. Yeah. I'd send him over there and play in my place sometimes. I had to go fulfill my job somewhere, like Mobile somewhere, I had to go and play. So we made good money on that coast. But see, O.G. Associates, every night I played over there, he wouldn't give me a nickel. See, when I get ready to come home, give me the whole thing, huh? Yeah. Pee right now.
Well that's a good idea.
Yeah, he wouldn't let me spend nothing, you see?
Yeah.

I wouldn't spend something, he wouldn't let me. I'm telling you, you go bring this money home to Miss Lucia. That's what he'd take. Yeah, I had a fine wife, she's dead. I married again, I got another fine wife. You see that? Yeah. You ever been to him? Yeah.
Yeah, I knew you, I'd be very much, very fine wife. Well I think that looks like the end of it there. Alright, you spell it. Wrap her up. Wrap her up.

segments.title: Opening, address and talk over photographs
segments.summary: Interviewers note the date (June 1961) and address, then look through Clayton's photographs, including a recent group picture and a country picnic job, with mic hum interruptions.

segments.title: Day job at Gramercy as a carpenter's helper
segments.summary: Clayton worked at Gramercy through the union local as a helper because music alone does not pay.

segments.title: Music is tough now; last job and Paul the drummer
segments.summary: Clayton says work is scarce; his last job was a short parade gig and a serenade for his father, and he mentions drummer Paul who plays with him regularly.

segments.title: Bands once hired for weddings and parties
segments.summary: The interviewer notes bands used to play every wedding and christening; Clayton says he once turned work away but things are rough now.

segments.title: Playing the lakefront camps and floods
segments.summary: Clayton played weekends at Milneburg camps, walking through backwater when storm tides flooded the boardwalk.

segments.title: Mama Lou's, Happyland and Mary's Camp on the lake
segments.summary: Clayton recalls leading a band with Andrew Jefferson at Mama Lou's, which closed after she died, plus Happyland and Mary's Camp, and the location of Lincoln Beach.

segments.title: A brawl at Mary's Camp
segments.summary: Clayton tells of a fight breaking out while the band played, hiding behind the music box while his brother-in-law sat on his head, and a young drummer fleeing.

segments.title: Brass bands: Supreme Band, Maurice Durand, Eureka and Cashmere
segments.summary: Clayton names trumpeters he played with and says he never led a brass band but joined the Eureka or John Casimir's band when hired.

segments.title: Excelsior band and Wooden Joe
segments.summary: He played with the Excelsior brass band and jazz band, and remembers Wooden Joe as a powerful trumpet player.

segments.title: Dan Moody's band on the Mississippi coast: a burned foot and a fall
segments.summary: Clayton toured with Dan Moody, sleeping in a hall by a fire where he burned his foot, and later fell off a bank with the band, wrecking instruments.

segments.title: Missed bus from Columbia and string of road accidents
segments.summary: He tells of chasing a Greyhound eight miles, a bus with bad tires, and several car wrecks, including one into a barbershop.

segments.title: Longer engagements at Mama Lou's during the Depression and after army
segments.summary: He describes steady Saturday and holiday work at Mama Lou's, pay and tips, raising the price after the army, and a drunk captain offering a hundred dollar bill.

segments.title: Lessons from Jim Humphrey and learning from Armstrong records
segments.summary: Clayton took lessons from Jim Humphrey with a method book, then learned tunes like Muskrat Ramble from Louis Armstrong records and turned down a road offer.

segments.title: Hard road trips with Earl Foster's band
segments.summary: He recalls hungry road trips and a string of car breakdowns with Earl Foster's Cadillac, ending with his deciding to drive his own car and give up the road.

segments.title: Playing in Chicago clubs
segments.summary: Clayton says he played Chicago spots like the Green Mill, Vendome, Sunset and Royal Garden, around the time Louis Armstrong was there.

segments.title: Tavern combo in Akron, Ohio, and coming home
segments.summary: Clayton played piano and trumpet in a small combo in Akron and toured Ohio and Pennsylvania before returning to New Orleans.

segments.title: Texas tours and a killing outside Orange
segments.summary: He describes train tours through Texas and a frightening night in Orange where the truck driver was shot and the band still had to play for cowboys.

segments.title: Good paying day jobs and giving up the road
segments.summary: Clayton recalls well paid jobs at Bramson's and the oil company, but says they do not last and he will not give up music.

segments.title: Playing at Bay St. Louis and closing remarks about his wife
segments.summary: He talks of his band at a Bay St. Louis hotel, a boss who held his pay for his wife, and his two marriages; the tape ends.
